story:
Portugal's national register of protected trees lists one Himalayan cedar in the whole of Porto, and it is not the one in the Palacio de Cristal gardens. It is this one, in a small university garden on Rua do Campo Alegre, beside the Palacete Burmester, the house the University of Porto now runs as the Casa dos Livros.

When the forest service measured it in 2020 it stood 23.5 metres tall, with a trunk 3.4 metres round and a crown 17.5 metres across. It was classified in one round with three neighbours in the same garden, a horse chestnut, a tulip tree and a yew. Four protected trees in one small garden looks like somebody planting with intent. No source names who, or when.

That silence runs all the way through. The register left the age column empty, and the city council's announcement of the classification gives no date either. A trunk of 3.4 metres says this cedar is mature. It does not say how mature, so this page prints no number, and the 2020 measurement is the latest anyone has published about it.

The garden sits on the Faculty of Sciences campus, a few hundred metres east of the Jardim Botanico do Porto, and no opening hours for it have been published. If you know when the Burmester garden was planted, or have an old photograph of this tree, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only cedar among the four protected trees here, 23.5 metres tall with a trunk 3.4 metres round. It stands in the Jardim do Palacete Burmester, with a horse chestnut, a tulip tree and a yew.

story:
Porto's most celebrated tree is a tulip tree at Casa Tait, protected since 1950 and put at more than 250 years old. A little over a kilometre west, in a university garden that hardly anyone writes about, stands another that Portugal's forest register measured at the same height, 36 metres. Its trunk is 4.9 metres round, against five at Casa Tait. Its age column is empty.

Matching measurements do not make matching ages, and nothing published dates this one. What the record does give is scale. The register measured it in 2020 with a crown 21.4 metres across, and it was classified in one round with three neighbours in the garden of the Palacete Burmester, the house the University of Porto now runs as the Casa dos Livros. The other three are a horse chestnut, a Himalayan cedar and a yew. Of the four it is by far the tallest, some twelve metres above the cedar.

Porto seems to collect these trees. A third giant tulip tree stands at Casa Allen, about 330 metres away, and a fourth on the lawn at Casa Primo Madeira.

Come in late October or November, when the leaves, cut square at the tip, turn clear yellow 36 metres up. The garden is on the Faculty of Sciences campus off Rua do Campo Alegre, a few hundred metres east of the Jardim Botanico do Porto; no opening hours for it have been published. If you know when this tree went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 36 metres, the tallest of the four protected trees in this garden, with a trunk 4.9 metres round. It stands in the Jardim do Palacete Burmester, with a horse chestnut, a cedar and a yew.

story:
Maia's council protects this cork oak for four reasons at once: its size, its structure, its age, and its cultural and historic setting beside a hilltop chapel. Portugal's forest service classified it in December 2010, after measuring a trunk 4.17 metres round, a height of 19.5 metres and a crown 15.4 metres across.

The register put it at 250 years at that measurement, which would make it about 266 now. Read that as an estimate rather than a count. Nobody has published how the figure was reached, so the honest answer is somewhere between two and three centuries.

The chapel beside it is harder to date than the tree. Visit Maia places the Capela de Santo Antonio around 1770 and tells a miracle legend about an ox cart and wine; another source puts the building in the twentieth century. No source ties the oak to the chapel's founding, so treat them as neighbours, not as a pair. Each June the Festa de Santo Antonio fills the hill around them.

The oak stands in the paved churchyard, walled in stone and reached by steps from Rua de Santo Antonio, inside an 18,000 square metre municipal green space. It is in Silva Escura, about 12 kilometres north of central Porto, and most people will come by car or taxi. The latest dated photographs of it were taken in July 2021. If you have stood under it since, tell us how it looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the cork oak beside the Capela de Santo Antonio, 19.5 metres tall with a trunk 4.17 metres round. It stands in the paved, stone-walled churchyard at the top of the steps from Rua de Santo Antonio.

story:
Portugal's tree register measures this bunya pine at 40 metres, taller than either of the two protected trees growing beside it. It is an Australian conifer, and it bears huge cones.

The forest service classified it as of public interest in May 2021, together with two neighbours, at the request of Porto's city council. The register gives a trunk 4.9 metres round, a crown 13.8 metres across and an age of about 150 years. It records no year for those measurements, so read the age as the register's estimate rather than a count. Somewhere between 120 and 180 years is the honest band.

The estate around it has a clearer date. In 1839 João Allen, British consul and wine merchant, bought Quinta de Villar d'Allen for a summer house and laid out an English-style landscape garden. His son Alfredo, the councillor in charge of the city's parks, helped bring about the Palácio de Cristal and moved many exotic trees from here into Cordoaria, Carregal and Passeio Alegre. Nobody wrote down which trees went in when, so this one cannot be tied to either man.

The garden still holds about 180 varieties of camellia, a lake, a glasshouse and a swan garden. It is not a walk-in park. Visits are guided and booked ahead, Monday to Saturday, through the estate on Rua do Freixo, about five kilometres east of the centre and some 275 metres from the Palácio do Freixo.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest of the three protected trees here, 40 metres, with a bunya pine's huge cones. It stands about 3 metres from the wide blue cedar and some 20 metres from the umbrella pine.

story:
This cedar grew out rather than up. Its crown spreads 20 metres across, half as wide again as that of the 40-metre bunya pine standing three metres away.

It is the blue form of the Atlas cedar, the cultivar Glauca, and Portugal's national register measures it at 32.75 metres tall with a trunk 4.3 metres round. The register gives an age of about 150 years but no year of measurement, so take that as an estimate, with somewhere between 120 and 180 as the honest range. The two trees stand so close that one stop covers both. Different species, different shapes, one patch of ground.

The forest service classified them, with a Japanese umbrella pine nearby, in May 2021, after Porto's council asked. They grow at Quinta de Villar d'Allen, the estate João Allen, a British consul who traded in wine, bought in 1839 and turned into an English-style landscape garden. The house and grounds have been protected as a monument since 2010. His son Alfredo, who ran the city's parks as a councillor, moved many exotic trees from here into Porto's public gardens. Whether either of them planted this cedar, no source says.

What the estate is known for now is camellias, about 180 varieties. Getting in means booking a guided visit, as the garden does not take walk-ins. The latest dated record of these trees is that 2021 classification, so if you have been round since, tell us how they look.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the blue needles of the Glauca form and a crown 20 metres across, much wider than its neighbour's. It stands about 3 metres from the 40-metre bunya pine, the taller of the pair.

story:
Japanese umbrella pines grow slowly, and this one has a trunk 3.15 metres round. That is the national register's figure, taken in 2021, and it is very large for the species. We found no second measurement to check it against, so it stands as the register's number until someone brings a tape.

Sciadopitys verticillata is not a true pine. It is the only living member of its own family, native to Japan, with needles set in whorls like the spokes of an umbrella. In Portugal it is a rarity. This one is 20 metres tall with a crown almost 14 metres across, and the register put its age at 151 when it measured it. That is the most precise age of the three protected trees on this estate and still an estimate, so read it as somewhere between 120 and 180 years.

The other two, a 40-metre bunya pine and a wide blue Atlas cedar, stand together about 20 metres away. Portugal's forest service classified all three in May 2021 at the request of Porto's council.

The ground is Quinta de Villar d'Allen, which João Allen, British consul and wine merchant, bought in 1839 for a summer house and an English-style landscape garden. His son Alfredo later sent many of its exotics out into the city's public gardens. No source says when this tree arrived, or who first brought a Japanese conifer to Porto's eastern edge.

Visits are guided and booked ahead, Monday to Saturday.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the smallest of the three protected trees, 20 metres tall with a trunk 3.15 metres round and needles in umbrella-like whorls. It stands about 20 metres from the bunya pine and the blue cedar.
